headline: Global investor interest in Australian private equity has materially increased, with local structural headwinds mild compared to the rest of the world
reasoning: Alex Ovchar observed at a major private capital conference in Singapore that the global investor community's interest in Australian private equity has materially grown. He noted that while local economic issues and structural headwinds exist, they appear very mild relative to challenges facing other global markets. This relative resilience is driving increased international capital allocation toward Australian private equity.
quote: I think it's interesting as at times when you're in the moment of the local economy, you see certain issues and structural headwinds in the global sense, they're actually very mild compared to what the rest of the world is going through. So for us, there's certainly an increase in interest in in our neck of the woods.

headline: Australia seen as a safe, distinctive macro environment with strong legal protections and less geopolitical risk than North America and Western Europe, making it attractive for global private equity capital
reasoning: Alex Ovchar argues that in an increasingly uncertain global environment, Australia is viewed as a stable, well-governed Western economy with strong institutions and relatively low geopolitical exposure. This macro stability is combined with a notably underpenetrated private equity market: PE represents less than 14% of total Australian M&A activity, versus 31% in the US and over 40% in Western Europe. This combination of stable backdrop and low competition creates better buying opportunities. Australian PE has delivered average returns of 15% over the last 5–10 years, materially above North American and Western European benchmarks, and with lower return dispersion/volatility than peer markets.
quote: In an increasingly uncertain global world, Australia's really seen as a very safe, distinctive environment to invest in. We're clearly not immune to a lot of the global shocks, but in many respects the protections we have as a Western economy, lots of legal protections, strong institutions, less exposure to some of the geopolitical risks that we see in North America and Western Europe as well as candidly the social and political issues as a result provide a very strong macro backdrop. What's more interesting is if you look into the private equity market specifically, despite that positive macro backdrop remains relatively under penetrated, IE the level of private equity activity is a lot less than we see in other markets. One way to think of it is as a percentage of total M&A activity less than Australia of total M&A activity within the Australian market, private equity represents less than 14%. If we look at other markets elsewhere, the US is 31%, Western Europe and parts of the UK are north of 40%.

headline: Individual investor access to Australian PE is growing; education and product access are the two key enablers; distinguishes PE from private credit liquidity concerns
reasoning: Ovchar notes that retail and high-net-worth individual access to private equity is rising globally and Australia is following that trend. Pacific Equity Partners has had individual investors since inception but is seeing a material increase in unsolicited interest from individuals it has not previously worked with. He frames the two priorities as education (helping investors understand risk/reward across the PE spectrum) and facilitating access through appropriate product structures. He also distinguishes PE from private credit, noting PE's longer-term 5–10 year horizon avoids the liquidity trap concerns being raised around private credit.
quote: There's been a material increase in individuals that we do not know or haven't worked with approach us with the desire to invest. And for us, what's important is 2 elements, one is education, making sure that we can explain the risk reward across the private equity spectrum so investors can make informed decisions about what's appropriate for them. But secondly is actually access and what's been an important investment for us but can't leave the industry is facilitating individual access to private equity products, which is rising globally and Australia's following that trend.

headline: Australian PE has delivered ~15% average returns over 5–10 years, above US and Western European benchmarks, with lower volatility — higher return and lower risk together, not in the usual trade-off
reasoning: Alex Ovchar highlights that Australian private equity has historically outperformed other Western markets on a risk-adjusted basis. Average returns of 15% over the last 5–10 years exceed those in North America and Western Europe. Unusually, this higher return has come with lower return dispersion — i.e., lower risk — rather than the typical trade-off between risk and return. This makes Australia a distinctive opportunity for international LP capital.
quote: The average private equity returns in the last 5, 10 years for the market have been 15%, which is materially above where other Western markets have been, both North America and Western Europe. But interestingly, that high return has come with lower risk dispersion or effectively lower risk. So while that's too often go hand in hand, if you look at the Australian private equity market, it's both being a stronger performing market, but also one with relatively less volatility than other markets.

headline: Value creation at PEP driven more than 75% by earnings growth; debt contributes less than 10% — rejects leveraged-buyout-style financial engineering as the primary return driver
reasoning: Ovchar pushes back on the perception that private equity returns are primarily driven by leverage and multiple expansion, calling it a caricature of how the industry operated in the US in the 1980s. He states that over the last 10–20 years, more than three-quarters of PEP's value creation has come from earnings growth, while debt accounts for less than 10%. The investment approach focuses on buying safe, defensive, market-leading businesses and doubling profits through operational improvements, margin expansion, and earnings growth rather than financial engineering.
quote: For us ultimately it's about earnings growth. That's sort of what we back. If we look at the value creation by source over the last 10 or 20 years, more than 3/4 of that within our firm comes from earnings growth, while debt represents less than 10%. It's a driver, but absolutely not the main driver of what drives our performance for us. And that's where we spend most of our time is how do we grow the earnings, not can we financially engineer an outcome that can give us a short term return.
